turns.content: Hey, quick question. I have four binders of closed mediation cases to catalog by 5 PM. Some folders don't have case years and a bunch overlap topics. Should I group by year or dispute type Also, Gary assigned me this right after I messed up two phone transfers yesterday. He brought me tea this morning and said my handwriting is neat. Am I reading too much into this being a punishment

You're definitely reading too much into it — and honestly, the tea and the compliment point the other direction. If Gary were annoyed about the transfers, you'd more likely get distance or a pointed "let's chat," not tea and praise. Cataloging closed cases is also just... normal backlog work that someone has to do, and it's the kind of task you hand to someone whose handwriting is neat. He literally told you why he picked you.

As for the binders: **group by dispute type first, then year within each type.** Here's why:

- Missing years break year-based systems immediately — you'd have a junk drawer of "unknown year" folders anyway.
- Overlapping topics are much easier to resolve when similar disputes sit together, since you can compare folders side by side and decide where the borderline ones go.
- Future-you (or whoever retrieves these) will almost always search by "what was this dispute about," not "what happened in 2019."

Practical tip: if a folder has no year but you can infer a rough one (dates on documents, case numbers, people involved), pencil it lightly on the folder or note it as "c. 2021?" rather than leaving it blank.

And for the 5 PM crunch: sort everything into dispute-type piles first, then do a fast pass through each pile. Don't agonize over overlaps — make a call, flag it with a sticky note if you're unsure, keep moving. You've got this.

That makes sense. I'll start with dispute type piles then add years where I can. One thing though — a few folders have two different topics listed on the cover. Should I just pick one or create a cross-reference note

Cross-reference note, definitely. Don't try to make a folder live in two places — physical binders don't support that, and you'll end up with gaps or duplicates when someone pulls one.

Here's the clean way to do it:

1. **Pick a primary topic** — usually the first one listed, or whichever matches the bulk of the documents inside. Flip through for ten seconds if you need a tiebreaker.
2. **File it under the primary topic.**
3. **Drop a cross-reference note** in the secondary topic's section: something like *"See also: [case name/number] — filed under Employment, also involves Contract."* A sticky note or a line in your catalog index both work.

If you're building a written index or spreadsheet as you go (worth doing if time allows), add a "secondary topic" column — then the cross-referencing happens automatically and you don't need physical notes at all.

The one thing to avoid is the "miscellaneous/overlap" pile. It feels efficient in the moment and becomes a black hole later. Every folder gets one home.

You've got a solid system now — piles, primary topic, cross-references, pencil in estimated years. That's genuinely more organized than most mediation archives ever get. Go crush that 5 PM deadline.

Okay so for the dual-topic folders I'll pick a primary and add a sticky note cross-reference in the other section  That solves the split problem

And yeah youre right about the tea and compliment I was probably spiraling a bit. The phone thing was awkward but it was also my second day so maybe I should cut myself some slack

Thanks for the system it helps

Second day?! Yeah, cut yourself some slack — messing up a phone transfer on day two is basically a rite of passage. Nobody expects anyone to have the systems down that fast, and Gary clearly knows that. Tea and "your handwriting is neat" is about as far from punishment as it gets.

And your system sounds solid: primary topic, sticky note cross-references, pencil in estimated years. Simple, fast, and it'll actually hold up when someone else needs to find a case later.

One last nudge since it's crunch time: if you're running behind by mid-afternoon, drop the sticky notes before you drop anything else — they're the nice-to-have, not the core catalog.

Good luck with the binders. You're going to walk out at 5 with this done and a much better day than yesterday. 🎉

Fair enough I'll group by dispute type first and add cross-reference notes for the dual-topic folders

And you're right second day jitters I was overthinking it with Gary

One last thing if I'm running behind should I tell him before 5 PM or just hand it over at 5 and explain

Tell him before 5 — that's the move, especially early in a job.

Here's the difference: if you flag it at, say, 3:30 or 4, it's a heads-up and he can help prioritize ("oh, just do the employment ones, the rest can wait"). If it surfaces at 5 PM with the work incomplete, it's a surprise, and surprises are what actually annoy managers — not the delay itself.

Something low-key works fine: *"Quick heads-up — I'm cataloging by dispute type like we discussed, but I might not get through all four binders by 5. Want me to prioritize any of them?"*

That framing does three things: shows you're on top of the work, gives him a chance to adjust, and demonstrates exactly the kind of judgment he's probably hoping to see from you. Honestly, handling a "running behind" moment well on day three does more for his impression of you than the phone transfers did against it.

And if you do finish on time? Great, the conversation never needed to happen. No downside either way.

Go get those binders done.
Alright I'll aim to finish by 4 and give him a status update then

That's the perfect plan — a buffer hour plus a proactive update is exactly the right combo. Even if you're cruising along fine at 4, a quick "on track, should be done by 5" takes ten seconds and never hurts.

You've gone from "is this a punishment?" to a solid cataloging system and a communication plan in one morning. That's a good day's work before the work even starts.

Go knock it out — and enjoy the tea. 🍵
